legal.hook: Judicial responses to climate change: Constitutionalising right to clean environment and protection against effects of climate change
legal.summary: The article examines judicial recognition of climate change as a constitutional matter in Indian courts. Bar & Bench reports on how Indian judges have begun framing environmental protection and the right to a clean environment as fundamental rights under the Constitution, rather than treating climate change as a purely policy or administrative issue. The piece tracks the trajectory of judicial intervention—from PIL benches recognizing environmental harm to more recent orders that anchor climate obligations directly in constitutional text (likely Articles 21 and 48A). The reporting indicates courts are moving beyond reactive pollution control to proactive climate impact mitigation, requiring state and corporate actors to demonstrate climate resilience in their operations. legal.contextNote: This reflects the Supreme Court's post-*Menaka Gandhi* (1978) expansion of Article 21 (right to life) to encompass environmental dignity, crystallized in cases like *MC Mehta v. Union of India* (1992) on air pollution. Article 48A (duty to protect environment) and the Environmental Protection Act, 1986, remain the statutory anchors, but courts increasingly read climate obligations as justiciable rights rather than mere directive principles. For in-house counsel at large corporates (especially energy/industrial groups like Reliance subsidiaries): (1) audit ESG disclosures and climate impact assessments against Article 21 framing—PILs can now target inadequate climate planning as constitutional violation, not just breach of pollution control rules; (2) monitor NCLT and High Court jurisdiction expansion—climate claims may be consolidated with corporate governance petitions under Company Law rather than siloed in environmental benches; (3) track whether MeitY/DPDP frameworks begin incorporating climate data governance (emissions tracking, carbon accounting) as part of data protection compliance.
